claim: The E. coli ribosome exit tunnel is approximately 100 Å long.
source: A large fraction of cellular proteins likely start to fold cotranslationally in the ~100 Å long exit tunnel in the ribosomal large subunit (Milligan and Unwin, 1986; Ban et al., 2000; Nissen et al., 2000), before they emerge into the cytosolic environment.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text with supporting citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In E. coli ribosomes, portions of the 23S rRNA and a few universally conserved proteins line the exit tunnel.
source: In E. coli ribosomes, portions of the 23S rRNA and a few universally conserved proteins line the exit tunnel, Figure 1A.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the ribosome structure.

claim: The tunnel proteins uL4, uL22, and uL23 consist of globular domains that are buried within the rRNA, and β-hairpin loops that protrude into the tunnel.
source: The tunnel proteins uL4, uL22, and uL23 consist of globular domains that are buried within the rRNA, and β-hairpin loops that protrude into the tunnel (Klein et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with a citation to Klein et al., 2004.

claim: The β-hairpin loops in uL4, uL22, and uL23 help stabilize the tertiary structure of 23S rRNA.
source: These loops help stabilize the tertiary structure of 23S rRNA (Lawrence et al., 2016) and contribute towards the unique geometry of the tunnel (Ban et al., 2000; Nissen et al., 2000; Harms et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The β-hairpin loops in uL4, uL22, and uL23 contribute towards the unique geometry of the tunnel.
source: These loops help stabilize the tertiary structure of 23S rRNA (Lawrence et al., 2016) and contribute towards the unique geometry of the tunnel (Ban et al., 2000; Nissen et al., 2000; Harms et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is stated with supporting citations.

claim: uL24 and uL29 are located near the end of the tunnel.
source: uL24 and uL29 are located near the end of the tunnel, and a hairpin loop in uL24 forms a finger-like structure that partially obstructs the tunnel exit port.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: A hairpin loop in uL24 forms a finger-like structure that partially obstructs the tunnel exit port.
source: uL24 and uL29 are located near the end of the tunnel, and a hairpin loop in uL24 forms a finger-like structure that partially obstructs the tunnel exit port.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: E. coli strains HDB143 (uL23 Δloop) and HDB144 (uL24 Δloop) are viable.
source: The E. coli strains HDB143 (uL23 Δloop; uL23 residues 65–74 deleted) and HDB144 (uL24 Δloop; uL24 residues 43–57 deleted) have previously been shown to be viable (Peterson et al., 2010), as is a strain where uL23 has been replaced by a homologue from spinach chloroplast ribosomes that also lacks the β-hairpin loop (Bubunenko et al., 1994; Bieri et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated with citations to previous studies demonstrating viability.

claim: In uL23 Δloop strain HDB143, uL23 residues 65–74 are deleted.
source: The E. coli strains HDB143 (uL23 Δloop; uL23 residues 65–74 deleted) and HDB144 (uL24 Δloop; uL24 residues 43–57 deleted) have previously been shown to be viable (Peterson et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: In uL24 Δloop strain HDB144, uL24 residues 43–57 are deleted.
source: The E. coli strains HDB143 (uL23 Δloop; uL23 residues 65–74 deleted) and HDB144 (uL24 Δloop; uL24 residues 43–57 deleted) have previously been shown to be viable (Peterson et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The loop deleted in the uL24 Δloop ribosomes does not interact with neighboring parts of the ribosome.
source: The loop deleted in the uL24 Δloop ribosomes does not interact with neighboring parts of the ribosome, Figure 2A, and hence its removal would not be expected to alter the structure of other parts of the exit tunnel.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: The removal of the uL24 loop would not be expected to alter the structure of other parts of the exit tunnel.
source: The loop deleted in the uL24 Δloop ribosomes does not interact with neighboring parts of the ribosome, Figure 2A, and hence its removal would not be expected to alter the structure of other parts of the exit tunnel.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference based on the lack of interactions.

claim: The loop deleted in uL23 Δloop ribosomes is located deep in the exit tunnel, approximately 40–50 Å from the exit.
source: In contrast, the loop deleted in uL23 Δloop ribosomes is located deep in the exit tunnel, Figure 2B, ~40–50 Å from the exit and it is not clear a priori whether its removal may cause rearrangements in other tunnel components.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: A cryoEM structure of the uL23 Δloop 70S ribosome was determined at an average resolution of 3.3 Å.
source: For this reason, we determined a cryoEM structure of the uL23 Δloop 70S ribosome at an average resolution of 3.3 Å, Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the structure and resolution.

claim: The shape of the tunnel remains unchanged in the uL23 Δloop ribosome when compared with wildtype E. coli ribosomes, except for an increase in volume resulting from the absence of the uL23 loop.
source: we determined a cryoEM structure of the uL23 Δloop 70S ribosome at an average resolution of 3.3 Å, Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and found that the shape of the tunnel remains unchanged in the uL23 Δloop ribosome when compared with wildtype (WT) E. coli ribosomes, except for an increase in volume resulting from the absence of the uL23 loop Figure 2C–D.
evidence: The claim is stated based on cryoEM structural analysis.

claim: Compared to WT E. coli ribosomes, the tunnel volume increases by 2,064 Å3 in uL23 Δloop ribosomes.
source: Compared to WT E. coli ribosomes, the tunnel volume increases by 2,064 Å3 in uL23 Δloop ribosomes, see Video 1, about 1/3 of the size of ADR1a (5,880 Å3) calculated by the same method.
evidence: The claim is stated with specific volume measurements calculated using POVME algorithm.

claim: The volume increase in uL23 Δloop ribosomes is about 1/3 of the size of ADR1a (5,880 Å3).
source: Compared to WT E. coli ribosomes, the tunnel volume increases by 2,064 Å3 in uL23 Δloop ribosomes, see Video 1, about 1/3 of the size of ADR1a (5,880 Å3) calculated by the same method.
evidence: The claim is stated with specific volume measurements.

claim: Translation rates in PURE are approximately 10 fold slower than in vivo.
source: Translation rates in PURE are ~10 fold slower than in vivo (Capece et al., 2015), but since the proteins studied here fold on micro-to-millisecond time scales, that is considerably faster than the in vivo translation rate, it is safe to assume that the folding reaction has time to equilibrate between each translation step both in vivo and in the PURE system.
evidence: The claim is stated with a citation to Capece et al., 2015.

claim: The proteins studied fold on micro-to-millisecond time scales.
source: Translation rates in PURE are ~10 fold slower than in vivo (Capece et al., 2015), but since the proteins studied here fold on micro-to-millisecond time scales, that is considerably faster than the in vivo translation rate, it is safe to assume that the folding reaction has time to equilibrate between each translation step both in vivo and in the PURE system.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text.

claim: The folding reaction has time to equilibrate between each translation step both in vivo and in the PURE system.
source: Translation rates in PURE are ~10 fold slower than in vivo (Capece et al., 2015), but since the proteins studied here fold on micro-to-millisecond time scales, that is considerably faster than the in vivo translation rate, it is safe to assume that the folding reaction has time to equilibrate between each translation step both in vivo and in the PURE system.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference based on the relative time scales of folding and translation.

claim: For WT and uL24 Δloop ribosomes, ADR1a ΔfFL starts to increase around L = 20–21 residues and peaks at L = 25 residues.
source: In the presence of Zn2+, the ΔfFL profiles for WT and uL24 Δloop ribosomes are very similar: ΔfFL starts to increase around L = 20–21 residues and peaks at L = 25 residues (gray and blue curves).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: For uL23 Δloop ribosomes, ADR1a ΔfFL starts to increase already at L = 17 residues and peaks at L = 21–24 residues.
source: In contrast, for the uL23 Δloop ribosomes, ΔfFL starts to increase already at L = 17 residues and peaks at L = 21–24 residues (red curve).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: The 29-residue ADR1a domain folds deep inside the ribosome exit tunnel in a location where it is in contact with the uL23 loop.
source: A previous cryo-EM study demonstrated that the 29-residue ADR1a domain folds deep inside the ribosome exit tunnel in a location where it is in contact with the uL23 loop (Nilsson et al., 2015), Figure 2B.
evidence: The claim is stated with citation to a previous cryo-EM study.

claim: The additional space available in uL23 Δloop ribosomes makes it possible for ADR1a to start to fold at 3–4 residues shorter linker lengths.
source: The additional space available in uL23 Δloop ribosomes makes it possible for ADR1a to start to fold at 3–4 residues shorter linker lengths (Lonset).
evidence: The claim is stated based on the experimental data comparing Lonset values.

claim: ADR1a folds approximately 9–12 Å deeper in the exit tunnel in uL23 Δloop ribosomes than in WT ribosomes.
source: Assuming an extended conformation of the linker segment (~3 Å per residue), ADR1a folds ~9–12 Å deeper in the exit tunnel in uL23 Δloop ribosomes than in WT ribosomes.
evidence: The claim is stated based on calculation from linker length differences.

claim: The 109-residue α-spectrin R16 domain has been shown to fold cotranslationally at L ≈ 35 residues, in close proximity to uL24 in the exit port region.
source: The 109-residue α-spectrin R16 domain has been shown to fold cotranslationally at L ≈ 35 residues, in close proximity to uL24 in the exit port region (Nilsson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: With both WT and uL23 Δloop ribosomes, R16 has Lonset = 31 residues and Lmax = 35 residues.
source: As seen in Figure 3B and Table 1, with both WT and uL23 Δloop ribosomes, R16 has Lonset = 31 residues and Lmax = 35 residues (gray and red curves).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3B and Table 1.

claim: For uL24 Δloop ribosomes, R16 has Lonset = 29 residues and Lmax = 33 residues.
source: For the uL24 Δloop ribosomes however, Lonset = 29 residues and Lmax = 33 residues (Table 1), suggesting that that spectrin R16 folds ~6–7 Å deeper in the exit tunnel when the uL24 loop does not obstruct the tunnel exit port.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Spectrin R16 folds approximately 6–7 Å deeper in the exit tunnel when the uL24 loop does not obstruct the tunnel exit port.

claim: The I27 domain folds at linker lengths L = 35–39 residues in close proximity to the uL24 loop.

evidence: The claim is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: The I27 fFL profile is not affected by the uL23 loop deletion.
source: The fFL profile is not affected by the uL23 loop deletion, but folding commences at ~4 residues shorter linker lengths in uL24 Δloop ribosomes, similar to R16 (Table 1).

evidence: The claim is stated based on analysis of fFL profiles.

claim: The uL24 loop prevents domains of Mw ≥10 kDa from folding inside the exit tunnel.
